The study examined 17 patients with MM who underwent spinal fusion for scoliosis correction without prior untethering procedures, despite all being radiographically tethered. The results showed excellent outcomes with successful correction of the mean Cobb angle from 82 degrees to 35 degrees (57% correction) and minimal complications. Only one patient experienced transient lower extremity weakness that resolved within one month, while no patients developed new cranial nerve palsy, shunt malfunction, urological changes, or upper extremity problems. The study specifically notes that untethering procedures carry significant morbidity risks including worsening neurological function and wound complications, suggesting that routine untethering may not be warranted when patients are not clinically symptomatic.

The study measured specific vertical distances from the tibial tuberosity to both the proximal (22 ± 4.4 mm) and distal (16 ± 4.4 mm) PCL footprint locations using MRI analysis of 223 knees. The researchers were able to calculate the probability of PCL removal based on these distance relationships, with only 5 knees showing 50% risk of entire PCL removal. This demonstrates that the tibial tuberosity provides consistent and measurable anatomical reference points that can reliably predict PCL footprint location during surgical planning.

The evidence strongly supports that preoperative tracheobronchoscopy (TBS) does matter in newborns with esophageal atresia. The study demonstrates that TBS was clinically useful in 28 out of 62 patients (45.2%), with the procedure being crucial in modifying the surgical approach in 15 patients (24.2%). Specifically, TBS identified 3 patients with previously undetected proximal fistulas who required a different surgical approach through cervical repair, and detected 4 cases of respiratory tree malformations that were not identified before the procedure. Additionally, TBS enabled mechanical occlusion of carinal fistulas in 14 patients to improve ventilation during repair, and no complications were observed from the procedure itself. These findings indicate that preoperative TBS provides significant diagnostic value and directly influences surgical decision-making in a substantial proportion of patients.

The evidence strongly supports that syncope during bathing in infants represents a pediatric form of water-induced urticaria. The study describes eight infants who experienced consistent symptoms upon water immersion - becoming pale, hypotonic, still and unreactive - with rapid recovery after removal from the bath. The researchers explicitly considered "an equivalent of aquagenic urticaria" as their hypothesis after ruling out seizures and gastroesophageal reflux. Supporting evidence includes the presence of dermographism in all six tested infants, family histories of water/sun-related skin reactions, and elevated blood histamine levels after bath exposure in the two infants tested. The favorable evolution after avoiding baths and the long-term follow-up showing continued water/sun sensitivity in some children further supports this being a pediatric manifestation of aquagenic urticaria.
